book.title: Competing Against Luck: The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice
book.author: Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, David S. Duncan

chapterBreakdown.gentle: One well-understood hire is useful, but it is not yet a resume. This chapter says a solution builds a kind of record through the jobs it keeps getting hired to do again. That record is more trustworthy than a slogan because it comes from repeated buyer choices. If the same progress keeps being trusted to the same offering, the pattern starts to show what the offering is really known for in practice. The chapter keeps the metaphor narrow. It is not about a literal job resume. It is about earned hiring history. One good story is too thin. Repeated hiring matters because it shows which kind of progress buyers reliably expect the solution to deliver over time. It also helps the reader see why repeated trust says more than a polished description ever can, especially when memory would otherwise overvalue one vivid case.
chapterBreakdown.direct: One interpreted hire can sharpen attention, but it still leaves the team with only a single data point. Chapter 6 pushes beyond that limit by asking what repeated hiring reveals over time. A solution's real identity is not defined by what the team claims about it, but by what buyers repeatedly trust it to do. The chapter uses the metaphor of a resume for that accumulated hiring record. A resume is built through repeated evidence, not through feature language alone. If similar buyers under similar pressures keep hiring the solution for the same progress, that pattern becomes stronger evidence than one vivid anecdote. The chapter also keeps a limit in place: one isolated success does not create a durable resume, and repeated use still has to be checked to see whether the same job is really being rehired across situations. In that sense, the resume is less a marketing summary than a disciplined record of what trust has already been earned in the market.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: A single good hire can flatter a team, but it cannot yet prove a resume. This chapter forces a harder standard. A solution earns its real standing through the jobs buyers keep rehiring it to do. That repeated trust matters more than feature swagger or positioning talk because it comes from behavior, not self-description. If the same progress keeps pulling buyers back under similar pressure, the resume starts to reveal itself. If not, the team may just be worshipping a lucky story. The chapter also refuses to turn the metaphor into fluff. A resume is not brand theater. It is a record earned through repeated hiring, and weak teams get into trouble when they confuse one proud case with a durable job identity. The market keeps the score here, and the market does not care about internal vanity or spin.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
One well-understood hire can teach something important, but it still does not amount to a resume. That is the pressure Chapter 6 answers. Once the team can hear one hiring decision more clearly, the next task is to notice what happens when similar decisions keep recurring. If buyers repeatedly trust the same solution for the same kind of progress, the solution starts to build a record of what it is genuinely relied on to do.

The chapter uses the word resume for that record, but the metaphor has to stay narrow. It does not mean a literal employment document, and it does not mean a broad brand story. It means accumulated hiring evidence. A solution's real standing is built through the jobs it keeps getting rehired for, not through the identity its maker prefers to advertise.

That is why repeated hiring matters more than one vivid anecdote. A single success can still be accidental, narrow, or misleading. But when the same progress keeps getting trusted to the same offering across situations, the team gains stronger evidence about what buyers actually expect from it. The repeated pattern becomes a more durable guide than one polished customer story.

The chapter also keeps a limit in place. Repetition alone is not enough if the team is lumping different jobs together too quickly. It still has to ask whether the same kind of progress is really being rehired or whether the offering is serving several different jobs that only look similar from a distance. A strong resume emerges from consistent hiring logic, not from sloppy aggregation.

Once the resume is clearer, the team can compare earned trust with aspiration. It can see what the product is truly known for, where expansion ideas fit or strain that record, and why later organizational choices need to align around the jobs that have actually been earned. That is the bridge toward the next section of the book. It reminds the reader that repeated buyer behavior is the evidence that later organizational choices have to respect.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
One interpreted hire can point the team in the right direction, but it cannot yet establish identity. Chapter 6 turns that initial insight into a sequence of repeated hires and asks what the pattern says about what buyers really trust. A solution's real identity is not established by what the team says about it, but by what buyers repeatedly trust it to do. The chapter calls that accumulated hiring record a resume.

The metaphor only works if it stays evidence-based. A resume is narrower and more earned than positioning language. It reflects the jobs an offering has actually been hired to do across repeated situations, not the full list of capabilities the company wishes to promote. Repeated hiring therefore becomes a stronger signal than a persuasive tagline or one memorable case.

This is why one story is too weak. A single hire can be informative, but it does not prove a durable pattern. When similar buyers under similar pressures keep rehiring the offering for the same progress, the team begins to see what kind of trust the market has actually granted. That trust record can confirm the product's intended identity, or it can expose that the market is using the offering more narrowly than the team believed.

The chapter also refuses a lazy reading of repetition. Repeated use is not enough if the team is collapsing distinct jobs into one flattering narrative. It still has to test whether the same progress is truly being served across those cases. Otherwise the resume becomes a storytelling device instead of an analytical tool.

That distinction matters strategically because the earned record can discipline expansion ideas. It helps a team see whether an adjacent move extends trust buyers have already granted or whether it asks the market for a leap that has not been earned. It also clarifies why redesigns can misfire when they erase the specific progress buyers had learned to expect.

Once the earned record is clearer, the organization has better material for later decisions. It can align around the jobs the offering has actually earned, not just around internal hopes. That is the setup for the next chapter, where the book turns toward integrating around a job instead of merely describing it.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A team that treats one good customer story like a resume is still running on vanity. Chapter 6 pushes back hard on that mistake. A solution earns its standing through the jobs buyers keep rehiring it to do, not through the cleverness of one case or the ambition of its messaging.

That is why the resume metaphor matters. It gives the team a way to name accumulated hiring history without pretending the market believes every claim on the product page. The real question is simple: what kind of progress do buyers keep trusting this thing to deliver under repeated pressure? If the answer keeps recurring, the resume gets stronger. If not, the team may just be flattering itself with isolated wins.

Repeated hiring is harder evidence than one anecdote because it shows what buyers rely on consistently. It exposes what the offering is really known for in action, not what the company wishes it stood for. That can be clarifying and painful at the same time, especially when the earned resume is narrower than the official story.

The chapter also sets a trap warning. Repetition can be misread if the team jams several different jobs into one proud summary. The resume only deserves trust when the same hiring logic is genuinely recurring. Otherwise the pattern is fake and the strategy built on it will wobble.

A hard edge of the chapter is that the earned resume can embarrass the company. It may show that buyers trust the offering for a smaller, less glamorous job than the team hoped to own. It may also reveal that a proposed expansion is not an extension of earned trust but a demand for forgiveness from people who never signed up for that leap. That is useful pain, because strategy gets better when it submits to the rehire record instead of arguing with it.

Get this right and the team gains a disciplined record of earned trust. That record becomes the basis for the next organizational move, because firms should integrate around what buyers reliably rehire, not around slogans they would like the market to believe.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The previous chapter teaches the reader how to hear one hiring situation more clearly. Chapter 6 asks what happens when that clarity is repeated. A single well-interpreted hire can reveal a lot, but it still does not amount to a resume. The chapter exists to explain what becomes visible once similar hires keep happening and the same kind of progress is repeatedly trusted to the same solution.

The title gives the chapter its central metaphor, but the metaphor has to stay disciplined. Building a resume does not mean collecting flattering product language, assembling a list of capabilities, or borrowing the logic of a literal employment document. It means accumulating a hiring record. The solution's real standing emerges from the jobs it keeps getting hired to do under recognizable pressures, not from the story its maker prefers to tell.

That is why repetition matters so much here. One strong hire might still be accidental, unusual, or tied to a narrow circumstance that never recurs. Repeated hires, by contrast, suggest that buyers have learned something stable about what kind of progress the solution can be trusted to deliver. The chapter therefore treats repetition as a way of distinguishing a durable hiring pattern from a single impressive event.

But the chapter also protects itself from lazy pattern-making. Repetition by itself is not enough if the team is smearing several distinct jobs into one convenient narrative. The same product can be used often for different reasons. A real resume requires more than frequency. It requires evidence that the same kind of progress is being hired again and again across situations that are meaningfully comparable.

This gives the metaphor its sharpest value. A resume is narrower and more earned than positioning language. It reflects demonstrated trust, not aspiration. If the market keeps rehiring the offering for a certain kind of progress, that pattern becomes a stronger guide than broad claims about what the offering could do. If the market keeps using it for something else, the team has to respect that earned record even when it is less glamorous than the internal story.

The chapter therefore helps the reader judge fit more honestly. It can explain why some expansion ideas feel natural because they extend the earned hiring record, while others feel strained because they ask the market to grant trust the offering has not yet accumulated. It can also explain why some redesigns fail when they ignore what buyers had already come to rely on.

This placement matters before the book turns toward the jobs-focused organization. Integration requires a stable object to integrate around. A blurry sense of what the offering is really hired to do will not support later decisions about priorities, consistency, or coordination. The resume gives the organization a firmer picture of the job record that has actually been earned.

That clearer picture also disciplines internal debates about where the product should stretch next. It helps the team separate extensions of earned trust from moves that would require buyers to relearn what the offering is for. In that way, the chapter does more than summarize the past; it narrows the field of credible future action.

Once that picture is clearer, the book can move from demand interpretation into organizational consequence. The next chapter can ask how a firm should integrate around a job, because this chapter has done the prior work of clarifying what repeated hiring evidence says the offering is truly trusted for.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
One interpreted hire can sharpen the team's hearing, but it still leaves identity unsettled. Chapter 6 follows what happens when similar hires keep occurring and turns that repetition into a repeated hiring record. An offering's real identity is not established by one successful use or by whatever the team says about it. It is established by what buyers repeatedly trust it to do across comparable situations. The chapter names that accumulated record a resume.

The metaphor only works if it remains evidence-based. A resume is not a slogan, a product narrative, or a literal HR analogy. It is a shorthand for the jobs a solution has repeatedly been hired to do. That makes it narrower than capability claims and more earned than positioning language. The question is not what the company believes the offering can be. The question is what repeated hiring behavior says the offering already is in buyers' lives.

This is why one vivid story is too weak. A single interpreted hire may still be atypical, situational, or misleading. Repetition gives the chapter something stronger: evidence that the same kind of progress keeps getting trusted to the same solution. That recurring pattern can confirm that the product is really known for a certain job, or it can reveal that the market is using the product more narrowly than the team intended.

The chapter resists sloppy aggregation. Repeated use is not enough if several different jobs are being collapsed into one proud summary. Frequency alone does not establish a resume. The team still has to test whether the same progress, under meaningfully similar pressures, is truly being rehired. Otherwise it mistakes coincidence or category familiarity for stable hiring logic.

This gives the metaphor strategic weight. A clearer resume helps the team judge whether product ambitions extend an earned trust record or demand trust the market has not yet granted. It helps explain why some adjacent moves feel easy while others require far more buyer re-education than internal teams expect. The resume becomes a practical way to compare aspiration with evidence.

The chapter also clarifies why redesigns can be dangerous when they overwrite the exact progress buyers had come to expect. An organization can think it is modernizing the product while the market experiences the move as a betrayal of the earned record. The resume therefore acts as a constraint on internal enthusiasm as much as a guide to external opportunity.

This placement in the book matters. Organizational integration around a job only makes sense if the offering's earned job record is clearer first. A company cannot align around a job it has not identified in its own repeated hiring history. The resume is the bridge between demand interpretation and organizational design.

Once the offering's repeated hiring pattern is clearer, the next chapter can ask how a firm should integrate around serving that job consistently. Chapter 6 therefore turns repeated buyer trust into a usable object for later coordination, priorities, and structure.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A team that mistakes one flattering case for a resume is still high on its own story. Chapter 6 cuts through that. An offering earns its standing through the jobs buyers keep rehiring it to do, not through the brilliance of one anecdote and not through whatever the product page claims this quarter.

That is why the resume metaphor is useful. It names accumulated hiring history. It asks a hard question: what kind of progress do buyers keep trusting this thing to deliver when the pressure returns? If the same answer keeps showing up, the résumé gets stronger. If the pattern keeps slipping, the team may be staring at a lucky win and calling it identity.

This makes repetition tougher than celebration. One successful case can still be weird, temporary, or strategically irrelevant. Repeated hires show what the market has actually learned to rely on. They expose what the offering is truly known for in action, not what the company hopes it stands for in theory. That can be clarifying and painful at the same time, especially when the earned record is narrower than the official story.

The chapter also draws a hard line against fake pattern-making. Repeated contact is not the same as repeated job logic. Teams can lump different hires together because the summary sounds elegant, then build strategy on a pattern that was never really there. A real resume has to be earned through consistent progress being rehired under comparable pressure, not through frequency theater.

That is what gives the chapter its bite. The resume outranks messaging because buyers write it with their repeated hires. It tells the team where trust already exists and where trust is still fantasy. It explains why some expansion moves feel natural while others demand the market forgive a leap it never agreed to make. It also explains why redesigns can backfire when they erase the very thing the old resume had earned.

It also makes the chapter strategically unforgiving. A company can discover that its most reliable resume is built around a smaller, less glamorous job than leadership wanted to claim. It can learn that a flashy adjacent move is really a request for unearned trust. That hurts, but it is better than mistaking aspiration for evidence and building structure around a fiction.

The discipline here is not emotional modesty. It is becoming accurate enough to make better bets. Once the earned record is visible, the firm can stop wasting time on identity fantasies and start deciding which promises it can actually keep at scale. It can also decide which promises it should stop making altogether, and which markets no longer deserve expensive persuasion campaigns.

This placement is exactly why the next chapter needs this one. Firms should integrate around what buyers reliably rehire, not around internal slogans. Chapter 6 strips the story down to the earned record first so Chapter 7 can talk about alignment without floating free of evidence.

examples.title: Jonah Tests Whether the Claimed Identity Matches the Earned Resume

scenario.gentle: Jonah's team wants to expand into a new use case. He has to decide whether the move builds on the product's existing resume or ignores what buyers have actually trusted before.
scenario.direct: The decision is not just about capability. It is about whether the expansion fits the earned hiring record.
scenario.competitive: Jonah has to choose between extending the résumé and faking a promotion.

whatToDo.gentle: Compare the new ambition with the repeated jobs buyers have already hired the offering to do.
whatToDo.direct: Use the resume as a check on whether the next move extends earned trust or demands unearned trust.
whatToDo.competitive: Ask whether the market has already written the first line of this next claim.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says a clearer resume helps the team judge fit more honestly.
whyItMatters.direct: Expansion looks different once the offering's earned record is made explicit.
whyItMatters.competitive: Resume truth is a better judge than ambition.

examples.title: Ava's Redesign Breaks What the Campus Print Station Had Earned

scenario.gentle: Ava redesigns the campus print station around broader convenience. Students react badly because the station had really earned trust for dependable last-minute printing under stress.
scenario.direct: The redesign ignored the service's actual resume and tried to replace it with a broader identity.
scenario.competitive: Ava upgraded the story and broke the earned job record.

whatToDo.gentle: Check what repeated job the service had already earned before changing the experience around a broader idea.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the existing resume as evidence that should constrain redesign choices.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not wipe out the rehire pattern just because a bigger story sounds nicer.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says repeated trust can be damaged when teams ignore what buyers had actually come to rely on.
whyItMatters.direct: Resume logic helps explain why some redesigns fail even when they sound more ambitious internally.
whyItMatters.competitive: Erase the earned record and the market punishes the vanity move.

examples.title: Malik Tests Whether One Good Experience Deserves Resume Status

scenario.gentle: Malik has one excellent experience with a new meal-planning tool and feels tempted to say it has already become his answer for weekly planning.
scenario.direct: The tool may be promising, but Malik has to decide whether one good hire is enough to call it a real resume.
scenario.competitive: One smooth win is trying to sell Malik on a promotion it has not earned.

whatToDo.gentle: Wait to see whether the same kind of progress keeps being trusted again before naming a durable resume.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the first success as a clue, then test whether similar hires recur under comparable pressure.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the tool earn repeat trust before giving it the title.

whyItMatters.gentle: The chapter says one strong hire can matter without yet proving a stable hiring record.
whyItMatters.direct: This is the limit that keeps the resume metaphor tied to repeated evidence.
whyItMatters.competitive: One good day still does not make a résumé.

front.direct: What kind of evidence writes the record?

back.gentle: Repeated hires for the same kind of progress.
back.direct: Accumulated hiring evidence across recurring situations.

front.gentle: Why is one strong story too weak by itself?
front.competitive: Why is one win still soft?

back.gentle: One story cannot prove a durable hiring pattern.
back.direct: Repetition shows whether the same job logic keeps recurring.
back.competitive: One case cannot write the whole résumé.

front.gentle: How is a resume different from positioning language?
front.direct: Why is the earned record narrower than messaging?
front.competitive: Why does the slogan usually overreach?

back.gentle: A resume comes from repeated buyer trust, not from claims alone.
back.direct: The hiring record is more earned than the story the company tells.
back.competitive: The market's rehires outrank the copy.

front.gentle: What keeps repeated use from automatically defining one stable resume?
front.direct: Why must the team still test for the same recurring job?
front.competitive: What stops fake pattern from becoming fake identity?

back.gentle: The same kind of progress has to be recurring, not just repeated use in general.
back.direct: Frequency alone is too weak if different jobs are being collapsed together.

front.gentle: Why does the book need a clear resume before organizational integration?
front.direct: What later move depends on the earned hiring record?
front.competitive: Why must the firm know the résumé before it reorganizes?

back.gentle: The organization needs to know what job it has actually earned before aligning around it.
back.direct: Integration makes sense only once the repeated job record is clearer.
back.competitive: No earned record, no serious integration.
